A
The time-domain shows a signal's amplitude as it changes over time (like a waveform), while the frequency-domain shows which frequencies make up that signal and their respective amplitudes (like a spectrum).

C
The Fourier Transform is used to convert a signal from its time domain representation into the frequency domain, effectively breaking it down into the individual frequencies that compose it.

B
The frequency-domain representation shows which frequencies are present in a signal. A simple oscillating signal, like a sine wave, consists of a single frequency, which appears as a sharp peak or spike at that specific frequency value.

B
The Fourier Transform uses an integral to correlate the original signal against sine and cosine waves of every possible frequency. The result of this process reveals the amplitude and phase of each frequency component, showing exactly how much each simple wave contributes to the original, complex signal.

B
The Fourier Transform is a mathematical tool that breaks down a signal (like an audio wave) into its individual frequencies. This is essential for digital signal processing, allowing software to identify and remove unwanted frequencies (noise) or to recognize the unique frequency patterns of specific sounds or words.
